intro: Faith does not ask you to switch off your mind. The Church teaches that faith and reason are like two wings that lift us toward the truth. Here are honest answers to the questions people really ask, with the reasoning laid out step by step, the strongest objections named fairly, and where to read more.

road.title: The road of reasons
road.about: Many people come to faith one step at a time. Each step rests on the one before it, like stones across a river. You can start anywhere, but this is the usual order.

steps.title: There is a God
steps.about: Reason alone can show that the world depends on a Creator who is wise and good.

steps.title: God has spoken in Jesus
steps.about: Jesus is a real person of history who claimed to be God, and the evidence that he rose from the dead is strong.

steps.title: Jesus founded a Church
steps.about: He did not leave a book or a set of ideas. He gathered apostles, gave them authority and promised to stay with them.

steps.title: That Church is the Catholic Church
steps.about: The community he built on Peter and the apostles still lives, unbroken, in the Catholic Church today.

steps.title: Come and see
steps.about: Reasons can bring you to the door. Faith is walking through it: trusting a Person who has already come looking for you.

method.title: When a doubt comes: five steps
steps: Name the question exactly. "Everything feels unsure" is hard to answer. "How can a good God allow cancer?" can be thought through.
Separate the question from the mood. Tiredness, grief or a bad week can make true things feel false. Feelings are real, but they are not arguments.
Look at the best case on both sides. Read the strongest objection and the strongest reply, not a cartoon of either.
Ask what the evidence as a whole points to. One hard question does not cancel ten good reasons.
Keep walking while you think. Pray honestly, even "God, if you are there, show me", and bring the question to your catechist, sponsor or a priest.
method.quote: Ten thousand difficulties do not make one doubt.

topics.q: Is it wrong to have doubts?
topics.short: No. Asking questions is part of a living faith, and the Church welcomes honest searching. What matters is what you do with a question: look for the truth, or push it away. Seeking the answer is already a way of taking God seriously.
steps: There is a difference between a question and a refusal. A question says "I want to understand". A refusal says "I will not believe whatever the answer is". The first is healthy; the second closes the door.

Great believers had hard questions. Thomas wanted to touch the wounds. Job argued with God. Saint Teresa of Calcutta lived for years without feeling God's presence. None of them were thrown out for asking.
The Church holds that truth cannot contradict truth. If God made both the world and the mind, then honest thinking can only bring you closer to him, never further away.

A difficulty is not the same as a doubt. You can find something hard to understand, like the Trinity, and still trust that it is true, just as you trust a doctor without understanding all of medicine.
So the right response to a doubt is not panic and not silence. It is study, conversation and prayer, all at once.

objections.o: If I really had faith, I would never doubt.
objections.r: Faith is not a feeling of certainty that never wavers. It is a choice to trust God, made with the mind and the will. That choice can be made on days you feel sure and on days you feel nothing.

objections.o: Doesn't the Church just want me to stop asking?
objections.r: The Church has written thousands of pages answering questions, from Saint Augustine to Saint Thomas Aquinas to the Catechism. It invites questions because it is confident about the answers.

topics.think: What is the one question that bothers you most right now? Write it down exactly, in one sentence.

scripture.note: Thomas asks to see, and Jesus meets him
"I believe; help my unbelief!"
Always be ready to give a reason for your hope

sources.title: Saint John Henry Newman, Apologia pro Vita Sua, chapter 5
Pope Francis, Lumen Fidei (The Light of Faith)

topics.q: Isn't faith just believing without evidence?
topics.short: Not in the Catholic sense. Faith is trusting someone for good reasons. Reason shows that God exists and that the Gospel is credible; faith then trusts what God reveals that reason could not find on its own.
steps: Most of what we know, we know by trusting others. You believe that your great-grandparents existed, that Antarctica is real and that your medicine is safe, mostly on the word of reliable witnesses.
Trust is reasonable when the witness is reliable. We do not trust everyone; we ask whether the person knows and tells the truth.

For God, reason can do two jobs. It can show that God exists (see the next section), and it can test whether a claim to speak for God is credible, through fulfilled prophecy, miracles, the holiness of the Church and the way the Gospel answers the human heart.

Then faith goes further. It trusts God about things reason could not discover alone, such as the Trinity or the Eucharist. That is not against reason; it is reason trusting the most reliable witness there is.
So Catholic faith is neither blind nor a mathematical proof. It is like a well-founded marriage: you have good reasons to trust, and then you give yourself.

objections.o: Science only believes what can be measured. Faith should too.
objections.r: The claim "only what can be measured is real" cannot itself be measured. Science is wonderful at its job, but love, justice, meaning and the reliability of logic are known in other ways too.

objections.o: The Church condemns people who think for themselves.
objections.r: The First Vatican Council actually condemned the opposite error, fideism, which says reason cannot know God at all. Catholics are told to use their minds.

topics.think: Name three things you believe because you trust someone. What makes that trust reasonable?

scripture.note: God's power is seen in the things he has made
Faith is the assurance of things hoped for
These signs are written so that you may believe

sources.title: Saint John Paul II, Fides et Ratio (Faith and Reason)
G. K. Chesterton, Orthodoxy (free e-book)

topics.q: What if I don't feel God at all?
topics.short: Feelings come and go, and they are not the measure of faith. Many saints went through long seasons of dryness. God's presence is a fact, not a mood, and he often works most deeply when we feel the least.
steps: Feelings follow sleep, health, stress and personality. They are real, but they are poor instruments for measuring whether God is near.
Love in any relationship is proven by faithfulness more than by feelings. A parent caring for a sick child at three in the morning may feel only tired, and still love completely.
The saints describe a "dark night": a time when prayer feels empty. Saint John of the Cross taught that this is often God weaning us off the feelings so that we love him, not just the comfort.
Catholic faith gives you anchors that do not depend on feelings: the sacraments, the Scriptures and the community. Christ is truly present in the Eucharist whether you feel it or not.
So keep praying, even a little, even dry. Faithfulness on grey days is a gift you give God.

objections.o: If God were real and loving, he would let me feel him.
objections.r: Sometimes he does, and that is a gift. But a love that depended on constant feelings would be fragile. God respects our freedom and lets love grow strong by being chosen.

objections.o: Other people seem to feel so much. Maybe something is wrong with me.
objections.r: People differ. Some are moved easily; others think their way to God. Both are normal. Talk with a priest or your sponsor, and also take care of yourself: sometimes dryness is linked to exhaustion or low mood that deserves care too.

topics.think: When have you loved someone faithfully even when you did not feel like it?

scripture.note: God in the gentle whisper, not the earthquake
His mercies are new every morning
Blessed are those who have not seen and yet believe

sources.title: Saint John of the Cross, The Dark Night of the Soul
Catechism 2725-2745: the battle of prayer

topics.q: Can reason show that God exists?
topics.short: Yes. The Church teaches that human reason can know with certainty that God exists, from the world he made. The simplest path: everything around us depends on something else to exist, and that chain cannot go on forever without something that simply exists by its own nature. That is what we call God.
steps: Look at anything: a tree, a star, yourself. It exists, but it does not have to. It depends on other things: parents, food, air, the laws of physics.
Those things depend on others in turn. Every item in the universe is "borrowed" existence, received from something else.
A chain of borrowing cannot explain itself. A train of a million carriages, with no engine, does not move. Adding more carriages does not help.
So there must be something that does not borrow its existence: something whose very nature is to exist. Philosophers call it the necessary being, or the uncaused cause.

That being must be outside space, time and matter (since those all depend on something), immensely powerful (it holds everything in being) and the source of all order and goodness we find. This is what all people mean by God.
Saint Thomas Aquinas gave five such paths, from motion, causes, dependence, degrees of goodness and the order of nature. Each one starts from something you can see and reasons to God.

objections.o: Maybe the universe itself is the necessary thing.
objections.r: The universe is made of parts that change, begin and end, and its laws could have been otherwise. A whole made of dependent parts is still dependent. Something that simply exists by nature cannot change or be otherwise.

objections.o: This only gives a "first cause", not the God of the Bible.
objections.r: True, and that is all it claims. Reason brings you to a Creator who is one, eternal and all-powerful. To know his name and his love, we need him to speak, which is the next step on the road.

objections.o: Why not an infinite chain of causes?
objections.r: Even an infinite chain of borrowers never explains why there is anything to borrow at all. The question is not "what came first in time?" but "what holds everything in existence right now?"

topics.think: Does anything you know of exist just by its own nature, needing nothing else? If not, what does that suggest?

scripture.note: God's invisible power is seen through creation
From the beauty of creation we come to know its Maker
In him we live and move and have our being

sources.title: Saint Thomas Aquinas, the five ways (Summa, I, question 2, article 3)
Peter Kreeft, Twenty Arguments for the Existence of God
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: the cosmological argument

topics.q: Did the universe have a beginning, and does it matter?
topics.short: Modern cosmology points strongly to a beginning about 13.8 billion years ago. Whatever begins to exist has a cause. A cause of all space, time and matter must itself be beyond them: timeless, immaterial and powerful. The Big Bang theory was first proposed by a Catholic priest.
steps: Whatever begins to exist has a cause. Nothing comes from nothing: not a rabbit, not a planet, not a universe.

The evidence of physics points to a beginning: the universe is expanding, the background radiation from its early hot state is still measurable, and the laws of heat say it cannot have been running down forever.
So the universe had a cause.
That cause cannot be part of the universe. It must be outside space and time (because it made them), not made of matter, and enormously powerful.
It also seems to be personal: only a choice explains why a timeless cause would produce a universe that begins, instead of nothing or something that always existed.
Father Georges Lemaître, a Belgian priest and physicist, first proposed what became the Big Bang theory in 1927. He saw no conflict between his science and his faith.

objections.o: Quantum physics shows things can pop into existence from nothing.
objections.r: The quantum vacuum is not nothing. It is a field full of energy, governed by laws. "Nothing" means no space, no energy, no laws at all. Physics studies what exists; it cannot explain why anything exists.

objections.o: Maybe there were endless universes before this one.
objections.r: That is speculation without evidence so far, and well-known results in cosmology suggest that even an expanding "multiverse" would still need a beginning. And even an eternal universe would still be dependent, as the previous topic shows.

topics.think: If there was once no space, time or matter, what kind of cause could bring them into being?

scripture.note: In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth
All things came into being through the Word
What is seen was made from what is not visible

sources.title: Georges Lemaître, priest and father of the Big Bang (Wikipedia)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: the cosmological argument

topics.q: Is the universe fine-tuned for life?
topics.short: Physicists have found that many basic numbers of nature, like the strength of gravity and the mass of the electron, sit in a very narrow range that allows life. Change them slightly and there would be no stars, no chemistry, no us. The best explanation is a mind that intended life.
steps: The universe runs on a few dozen constants, numbers that physics measures but does not explain.

Many of them have to be just right for life. If the strong nuclear force were a few percent different, there would be no stable atoms beyond hydrogen, or no hydrogen at all. If the cosmological constant were larger by a tiny fraction, matter would never have clumped into galaxies.
There are three possible explanations: necessity (they had to be this way), chance (we got lucky) or design (they were set this way on purpose).
Necessity has no support: physics knows of no reason these values could not be different.

Chance is extraordinarily unlikely. It is like a sniper firing a hundred rifles at you and every bullet missing. Saying "if they had hit, you wouldn't be here to wonder" doesn't remove the need for an explanation.
Design fits best. A universe ready for life from the start is what we would expect if a good and intelligent Creator wanted creatures who could know and love him.

objections.o: There could be countless universes, and we happen to live in the lucky one.
objections.r: No other universe has ever been observed. And a machine that produces universes with varying laws would itself need fine-tuning. It moves the question back a step without answering it.

objections.o: Life would just adapt to different conditions.
objections.r: The point is deeper than our kind of life. In most alternative settings there would be no stable atoms or long-lived stars, so no complex chemistry of any kind.

topics.think: If you found a planet with a working garden and every tap and dial set exactly right, what would you conclude?

scripture.note: The heavens declare the glory of God (Psalm 19 in most Bibles)
He formed the earth to be lived in
Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?

sources.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: fine-tuning
Peter Kreeft, Twenty Arguments for the Existence of God

topics.q: Can we be good without God?
topics.short: People who do not believe in God can certainly do good, and often do. The deeper question is why anything is really good or evil at all. If there is no God, moral rules are only opinions or instincts. If some things are truly wrong for everyone, always, that points to a moral law and a Lawgiver.
steps: We all know that some things are really wrong: torturing a child for fun, betraying a friend for money. Not just "I dislike it", but wrong, even if a whole society approved.
We also hold people to standards they did not choose. We say a dictator was evil, not merely that he broke local customs.

Physics and biology describe what is. They cannot, on their own, tell us what ought to be. Evolution can explain why we have feelings of guilt, but not why cruelty is actually wrong rather than just unpopular.
A real moral law that binds every person needs a source higher than any person or culture.
The best explanation is a personal God who is goodness itself, who made us for love and wrote his law on our hearts. Conscience is his voice in us.
So the moral sense everyone has is a clue: it points beyond us to the One who is Good.

objections.o: Morality is just what helps the species survive.
objections.r: If so, a cruel act that helped survival would be good, and self-sacrifice for a stranger would be foolish. Our conscience says the opposite, which suggests morality is more than survival.

objections.o: Cultures disagree about morals, so morals are relative.
objections.r: Cultures disagree on details, but nearly all share a core: honour parents, do not murder, keep promises, care for the weak. Disagreement also assumes there is a right answer to disagree about.

objections.o: Believers do terrible things too.
objections.r: Sadly, yes. But that shows people fail to live by the moral law, not that there is none. In fact, we only call it terrible because we know the standard.

topics.think: Is there anything you believe is wrong always, everywhere, for everyone? Where does that conviction come from?

scripture.note: The law written on the heart
I will write my law on their hearts
Do justice, love kindness, walk humbly with God

sources.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: moral arguments for God
Saint John Paul II, Veritatis Splendor (The Splendour of Truth)

topics.q: If God made everything, who made God?
topics.short: No one. The argument is not that everything needs a cause, but that everything that begins or depends on something needs a cause. God, by definition, does not begin and depends on nothing. Asking who made the Unmade is like asking who married the bachelor.
steps: Things that begin to exist, or that could fail to exist, need a cause.
But the chain of causes must end in something that does not need a cause, or nothing would ever exist (see "Can reason show that God exists?").
That uncaused reality is what we mean by God: eternal, with no beginning, existing by his own nature.
So "who made God?" is a question about a different kind of being: a made God would not be God, and we would have to ask about whoever made him.

Everyone, believer or not, has to accept something that just exists without a cause. The atheist says the universe; the believer says God. The question is which fits the evidence: a universe that changes, begins and depends, or a God who does not.

objections.o: That is special pleading: you exempt God from the rule.
objections.r: The rule was never "everything has a cause". It was "whatever begins or depends has a cause". God fits neither, so the rule does not apply. That is a definition, not an exemption.

objections.o: God would have to be more complex than the universe, so even harder to explain.
objections.r: Classical philosophy holds that God is perfectly simple: not made of parts, not built up out of pieces. He is not a very complicated machine but pure existence and pure act.

topics.think: What do you think has always existed: the universe, or God? Why?

scripture.note: "I AM WHO I AM"
The Alpha and the Omega, who is and was and is to come

sources.title: Saint Thomas Aquinas, the simplicity of God (Summa, I, question 3)
Peter Kreeft, Twenty Arguments for the Existence of God

topics.q: If God exists, why doesn't he make it obvious?
topics.short: God gives enough light to find him for anyone who seeks, but not so much that we are forced. Love must be free. A God who overwhelmed us with proof would get obedience, not love. And for those who look, he has made himself very near: in creation, in conscience, and above all in Jesus.
steps: God's goal is not only that we know he exists. Even demons know that. His goal is a relationship of love, which must be freely chosen.
If God appeared in the sky every hour, we would obey out of fear or pressure. Freedom to love needs some room to say no.
Yet God is not silent. Creation, the moral law in our hearts, the history of Israel, the life of Jesus and the witness of the saints are all signals for those willing to look.
Our own state matters too. Noise, distraction and pride can deafen us. Many people find that when they become still and honest, the signals grow clearer.
In Jesus, God did the opposite of hiding: he came close enough to be touched, eaten with and crucified. He came humbly, so as not to force anyone.

objections.o: Some sincere people search and never find him.
objections.r: We cannot see into anyone's heart or the end of their story. The Church teaches that God offers every person the grace they need, in ways we may not see, and many find him late in life.

objections.o: A loving parent would never hide from a child.
objections.r: A good parent also does not do everything for a child. Sometimes they step back so the child can grow and choose. God is near, but he waits to be welcomed, not forced.

topics.think: Have you been looking for God in a way that leaves room for him to answer quietly?

scripture.note: When you seek me with all your heart, you will find me
Seek and you will find
He is not far from each one of us

sources.title: Blaise Pascal, Pensées (free e-book)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: divine hiddenness

topics.q: If God is good, why is there evil?
topics.short: This is the hardest question, and no short answer removes the pain. But reason shows there is no contradiction between a good God and a world with evil. God made creatures free so that they could love, and freedom makes evil possible. God did not stay distant from it: in Jesus, he entered suffering himself and defeated it from the inside.
steps: Evil is not a thing God made. It is a lack: goodness missing where it should be, like a hole in a coat. God made everything good.
Much evil comes from free choices: war, cruelty, lies, injustice. God made us free because love must be free. A world of robots would have no evil and no love either.
A good God could allow evil if he can bring a greater good out of it. We often cannot see that good now, just as a child cannot see why the doctor gives a painful injection.
Notice that calling something truly evil assumes a real standard of good. Without God, suffering is just how the universe happens to be. The very protest against evil points toward the Good.

Christianity does not just explain suffering. It shows God suffering with us: Jesus was betrayed, tortured and killed unjustly, and then rose. The Cross is the place where the worst evil became the source of the greatest good.
The story is not over. God promises to wipe away every tear. Evil is real, but it does not have the last word.

objections.o: An all-powerful God could make free people who never choose evil.
objections.r: If God made our choices for us, they would not be ours. Making a being who is truly free and yet guaranteed never to choose wrong is like making a square circle: not a limit on God's power, but a contradiction.

objections.o: So much suffering seems pointless.
objections.r: It seems so to us, but we see only a sliver of history. If God exists and is infinitely wise, we should expect that we often cannot see his reasons. Faith trusts the One who proved his love on the Cross.

objections.o: I don't want an argument. I'm grieving.
objections.r: That is completely understandable. In grief, arguments help less than presence. The Bible gives whole books, like Job and Lamentations, to crying out to God. You can bring your anger and pain to him too.

topics.think: Where have you seen something good come out of something painful in your life or someone else's?

scripture.note: You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good
All things work together for good for those who love God
He will wipe every tear from their eyes

sources.title: Saint John Paul II, Salvifici Doloris (On Christian Suffering)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: the problem of evil

topics.q: What about earthquakes, illness and disasters?
topics.short: Not all suffering comes from human choices. Some comes from a world of real, stable laws, the same laws that make life possible. The Church also teaches that creation is unfinished and was wounded by sin. These answers do not make suffering small, but they show it is not a proof against God.
steps: A world where we can make free choices needs stable laws of nature. Fire that warms must also be able to burn; water that gives life can also drown.
The same processes that cause earthquakes, like the movement of the earth's plates, also recycle minerals and keep the planet fit for life.
God created the world "in a state of journeying": good, but not yet complete. It is moving toward a final perfection.
Scripture also teaches that sin has wounded creation and our relationship to it. We are out of harmony with God, each other and nature.
Disasters call out the best in people: courage, generosity, rescue, solidarity. That does not justify them, but it shows good can grow even there.
Above all, Christians do not believe in a God who watches from far away. Jesus healed the sick, wept at his friend's tomb, and promised a new creation where there will be no more death.

objections.o: Why couldn't God make a world without disasters?
objections.r: Perhaps a world with fixed, dependable laws is the only kind where free creatures can act, learn and grow. And God promises that this world is not the final one.

objections.o: Children get cancer. Nothing justifies that.
objections.r: We agree that it is terrible, and the Church spends enormous effort fighting disease through hospitals and research. Faith does not say suffering is good. It says God is with the suffering and will bring them to a life where it is undone.

topics.think: How does Jesus weeping at Lazarus' tomb (John 11:35) change the way you picture God when someone suffers?

scripture.note: Jesus weeps, then raises Lazarus
All creation groans, waiting for freedom
The tower that fell was not a punishment for sin

sources.title: Saint John Paul II, Salvifici Doloris (On Christian Suffering)
Catechism 302-314: providence and the scandal of evil

topics.q: How can a loving God allow hell?
topics.short: God does not want anyone to be lost. Hell is not God losing his temper; it is the state of a person who finally and freely refuses love. God respects our freedom to the very end. The doctrine of hell is a measure of how seriously he takes our choices.
steps: God is love, and he wants everyone to be saved. He sent his Son so that no one would be lost.
Love cannot be forced. If we are free to say yes to God, we must also be free to say no.
Heaven is life with God. A person who has finally rejected God would not want to be there; it would feel like torment rather than joy.
So hell is the self-chosen state of being cut off from God, the source of all good. The Church calls this "definitive self-exclusion".
The Church has declared many people to be in heaven (the saints) but has never declared that any particular person is in hell. We are called to hope and pray for everyone.

objections.o: Eternal punishment for a short life is unfair.
objections.r: Hell is not a sentence added from outside for a few mistakes. It is the lasting state of a soul that has fixed itself against God. Sin repented of, however great, is always forgiven.

objections.o: A loving God would just let everyone in.
objections.r: Forcing someone into a relationship they reject is not love. God's mercy is endless, but it must be received.

topics.think: What does it say about God that he will not force your heart, even to save you?

scripture.note: God desires everyone to be saved
Not wanting any to perish
The judgment of the nations

sources.title: Pope Benedict XVI, Spe Salvi (Saved in Hope), 44-47
C. S. Lewis, The Great Divorce (about the book)

topics.q: Did Jesus really exist?
topics.short: Yes. Almost every historian, believer or not, agrees that Jesus of Nazareth was a real Jewish teacher who was baptized by John and crucified under Pontius Pilate. The evidence for him is better than for many figures of the ancient world.
steps: We have four Gospels and the letters of Paul, all written within the lifetime of people who knew Jesus. Paul's earliest letters date from about 20 years after the crucifixion.

Non-Christian writers mention him too. The Roman historian Tacitus (about AD 116) writes that "Christus" was executed by Pontius Pilate under Tiberius. The Jewish historian Josephus (about AD 93) mentions "James, the brother of Jesus who was called Christ".
The Gospels name real places, rulers and customs that archaeology has confirmed, like the pool of Bethesda and an inscription with Pilate's name.
The first Christians were Jews who would never have invented a crucified Messiah. Crucifixion was a shameful death, the opposite of what they expected.
So the question for an honest person is not "did Jesus exist?", but "who was he?"

objections.o: The Gospels are biased because they were written by believers.
objections.r: Every ancient source has a point of view. Historians weigh such sources with care, and the Gospels pass many of their tests: early date, multiple independent accounts and details that were embarrassing to the authors.

objections.o: Jesus is just a copy of older myths, like Horus or Mithras.
objections.r: Specialists have largely rejected this. The supposed parallels are vague, come from later sources or were exaggerated. The Gospels are rooted in first-century Jewish life, not in pagan myth.

topics.think: If Jesus really lived, which of his words would you most want to hear for yourself?

scripture.note: Luke checked his sources carefully
An early list of witnesses
What we have seen and touched

topics.q: Was Jesus just a good teacher or a prophet?
topics.short: Jesus did not leave that option open. He forgave sins in his own name, claimed to be one with the Father, accepted worship and applied God's own name to himself. Someone who says such things is either deceived, deceiving or telling the truth. His life and his Resurrection point to the truth.
steps: Jesus said things no mere prophet says. Prophets said "Thus says the Lord." Jesus said "But I say to you."
He forgave sins against others, which only the one offended, ultimately God, can do. His listeners understood this: "Who can forgive sins but God alone?" (Mark 2:7).
He said "Before Abraham was, I AM", using the divine name from the burning bush, and people picked up stones because they understood him to claim to be God (John 8:58-59).
He accepted worship from Thomas: "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:28). A good Jewish teacher would have stopped him.

So there are three options. If his claims were false and he knew it, he was a liar. If false and he did not know it, he was badly deluded. If true, he is Lord. "Just a good teacher" is not one of the options.
His wisdom, his balance, his love for the poor and his willingness to die do not fit a liar or a madman. Then the Resurrection confirms the claim.

objections.o: Jesus never said "I am God" in those exact words.
objections.r: Not in one sentence, but in many ways that his Jewish audience understood perfectly, which is why he was accused of blasphemy and condemned. He claimed God's authority, God's name and God's honour.

objections.o: Later Christians added these claims.
objections.r: The claims are in the earliest sources, including Mark, the first Gospel, and Paul's letters from the 50s AD, which already worship Jesus as Lord. There was no time for a slow legend.

topics.think: If Jesus really said these things, what does that ask of you?

scripture.note: "Your sins are forgiven"
"Before Abraham was, I am"
Condemned for his answer to the high priest
An early hymn to Christ as God

topics.q: Did Jesus really rise from the dead?
topics.short: This is the centre of everything. A few facts are accepted by most historians, including sceptics: Jesus died by crucifixion, his tomb was found empty, many people, friends and enemies, were convinced they had seen him alive, and the movement exploded in the very city where he was killed. The Resurrection explains all of these better than any alternative.
steps: Jesus died by crucifixion. Roman soldiers were experts at execution, and both Christian and non-Christian sources report it.

The tomb was found empty. The first witnesses were women, whose testimony was given little weight then, so no one inventing a story would choose them. And Jesus' enemies did not produce the body; they claimed it was stolen.

Many people experienced appearances of the risen Jesus: Peter, the Twelve, more than 500 at once, his sceptical brother James and Paul, a persecutor of Christians. Paul passes on this list within a few years of the events (1 Corinthians 15:3-8).

The disciples were transformed from frightened men into bold witnesses, and many died rather than deny what they had seen. People die for things they believe are true, but not for what they know they made up.

Now weigh the explanations. Stolen body? It does not explain the appearances or the martyrs. Hallucinations? Groups do not share the same hallucination, and they would not explain the empty tomb. He didn't really die? A half-dead, scourged man would inspire pity, not worship.
The explanation that fits all the facts is the one the witnesses gave: God raised Jesus from the dead. And if he rose, his claims about himself are true.

objections.o: Dead people don't rise. That rules it out from the start.
objections.r: Dead people don't rise by natural causes, which is exactly what the disciples knew too. The claim is that God raised him. If God exists (the first step on the road), that is possible, and then it is a question of evidence.

objections.o: The stories in the Gospels differ in details.
objections.r: Independent witnesses always differ in details. Identical stories would suggest copying. They agree on the core: the tomb was empty on the first day of the week, women found it, and Jesus appeared to his followers.

topics.think: If the Resurrection really happened, what difference does it make to your life, your fears and your death?

scripture.note: If Christ has not been raised, our faith is in vain
The road to Emmaus
The empty tomb and Mary Magdalene
Peter preaches in Jerusalem, weeks later

sources.title: Catechism 638-658: on the third day he rose again
Pope Benedict XVI, Jesus of Nazareth: Holy Week (about the book)
Resurrection of Jesus: historical discussion (Wikipedia)

topics.q: Why did Jesus have to die?
topics.short: Sin is not a small mistake; it breaks our relationship with God, who is life itself. We could not repair it alone. Jesus, fully God and fully human, offered his whole life in love on our behalf. On the Cross, love absorbed the full weight of evil and returned only forgiveness, and the Resurrection shows that love won.
steps: God made us for friendship with him. Sin is turning away from that friendship, and it wounds us, others and the world.
A broken relationship cannot be fixed by the one who broke it simply saying "let's forget it". Real reconciliation means facing the harm honestly.
As a human being, Jesus could stand in our place and offer the perfect love and obedience that we failed to give.
As God, his offering has infinite worth. It is enough for every sin of every person.
The Cross does not show an angry God who needs blood. It shows a God who loves so much that he goes all the way into our darkness, even death, so that nothing can separate us from him.
God was not defeated. Three days later, Jesus rose. The Cross is not the end of the story; it is the door.

objections.o: Why couldn't God just forgive without the Cross?
objections.r: God could have chosen another way. Saint Thomas Aquinas says the Cross was the most fitting way, because it shows both the seriousness of sin and the depth of God's love, and it heals us by moving our hearts.

objections.o: God would not let his messenger be killed; maybe it only looked as if Jesus died.
objections.r: This is a sincere belief of many, including Muslims. But Jesus' death is among the best attested facts of ancient history, confirmed by Roman and Jewish sources. And in the Christian view, his death was not a defeat for God but God's own plan of love.

topics.think: What does it mean to you that Jesus would have died even if you were the only person who needed saving?

scripture.note: He was wounded for our sins
God so loved the world
While we were still sinners, Christ died for us
To give his life as a ransom for many

sources.title: Saint Thomas Aquinas on why the Passion was fitting (Summa, III, question 46)
Catechism 599-618: Christ's death in God's plan

topics.q: Three persons and one God: isn't that a contradiction?
topics.short: No. A contradiction would be one God and three Gods, or one person and three persons. Christians believe in one God (one "what") who is three Persons (three "who"). It is a mystery beyond full understanding, but not against logic. Christians are firmly monotheists.
steps: A contradiction says A and not-A in the same sense. "One God and three Gods" would be a contradiction. The Trinity says something else.
There is one divine nature, one being: one God. That answers the question "what is God?"
In that one God there are three Persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. That answers the question "who is God?"
We already know that "what" and "who" are different questions. You are one "what" (one human nature) and one "who" (one person). God is one "what" and three "who".
This fits what God revealed: Jesus prays to the Father, promises to send the Spirit, and yet says "the Father and I are one".
It also fits the deepest claim of all: God is love (1 John 4:8). Love needs a lover, a beloved and the love between them. From all eternity, before creation, God is a communion of love.

objections.r: That is true for three separate things added together. The Persons are not three parts or three gods added up. Each Person is the whole God, entirely. It is more like 1 x 1 x 1 = 1, though every picture falls short.

objections.o: The word "Trinity" is not in the Bible.
objections.r: The word is not, but the teaching is: one God (Deuteronomy 6:4), Jesus as God (John 1:1), the Spirit as God (Acts 5:3-4), and the three named together (Matthew 28:19). The Church chose a word to summarize what Scripture says.

objections.o: Christians worship three gods.
objections.r: Christians, like Jews and Muslims, confess that God is one. The Creed begins "I believe in one God". The Trinity is a teaching about the inner life of the one God, not a belief in many.

topics.think: What does it change to know that God is not lonely, but is a communion of love from all eternity?

scripture.note: The Lord our God is one Lord
Baptize in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit
The Word was God, and became flesh
God is love

sources.title: Catechism 232-260: the Holy Trinity
Saint Augustine, On the Trinity

topics.q: Can we trust the Bible?
topics.short: There are good reasons to. The New Testament is the best preserved text of the ancient world, written close to the events, and much of its history has been confirmed. Catholics also trust it because of who handed it to us: the Church that wrote it, recognized it and has guarded it.
steps: Has it been changed? We have more than 5,800 Greek manuscripts of the New Testament, some within a century or so of the originals. For most ancient books, we have a handful of copies from a thousand years later. Scholars can reconstruct the original text with great confidence.
Is it close to the events? The Gospels were written within roughly 30 to 70 years of Jesus, while eyewitnesses were alive. Paul's letters are earlier still.
Is it accurate? Archaeology has confirmed many people and places it mentions, like Pontius Pilate, the high priest Caiaphas and King David's dynasty.

Is it God's word? This is a matter of faith, but not blind faith. If Jesus rose from the dead and founded a Church (see those topics), we can trust the Church he founded when it tells us which books are inspired.
Catholics believe the Bible is inspired by God and teaches without error the truth God wanted written for our salvation. It is also truly human, written by real authors in real styles.

objections.o: The Bible was edited by councils that chose what they liked.
objections.r: The core books were already read and trusted by Christians everywhere long before any council. Councils recognized and confirmed what the Church already used, while rejecting later writings that did not fit the apostles' teaching.

objections.o: It's just a translation of a translation.
objections.r: Modern translations go straight back to the Hebrew and Greek manuscripts. Different translations differ in style, not in the message.

topics.think: Which book of the Bible would you like to read next to judge it for yourself?

scripture.note: All Scripture is inspired by God
We were eyewitnesses
An orderly account

sources.title: Dei Verbum (Vatican II on Divine Revelation), chapters 3-5
Pope Benedict XVI, Verbum Domini (The Word of the Lord)
Biblical manuscripts (Wikipedia)

topics.q: What about violence and contradictions in the Bible?
topics.short: The Bible is a library written over more than a thousand years, in many styles. Catholics read it as a whole, in its context, and in the light of Jesus. God revealed himself step by step to a people who were slowly learning, and the hard passages are part of an honest record of that journey.
steps: The Bible contains history, poetry, law, prophecy, letters and parables. Each must be read according to its kind, as we would read a poem differently from a news report.
God taught his people gradually, the way a teacher starts with simple lessons. Some Old Testament laws and practices reflect a stage of that teaching, not its final word.
Not everything the Bible describes, it approves. It records the sins of its heroes honestly, including David and Peter.
Many "contradictions" disappear on a closer look: different authors focus on different details, round numbers, or arrange events by theme rather than date.
The key that unlocks the whole Bible is Jesus. Hard passages are read in his light: he taught love of enemies and revealed what God is truly like.
Pope Benedict XVI wrote that the "dark" passages must be read with care, in context, with the help of the Church, and never used to justify violence today.

objections.o: If God inspired it, why is it so hard to understand?
objections.r: Because God respected his human authors and their cultures, and because deep truths take a lifetime to absorb. That is one reason Christ gave his Church to help us read it.

objections.o: The God of the Old Testament seems different from Jesus.
objections.r: It is the same God, revealed gradually. The Old Testament is full of mercy too ("I desire mercy, not sacrifice", Hosea 6:6), and Jesus himself warned of judgment. In Jesus, we see God's face fully.

topics.think: Is there a passage that troubles you? Write it down and ask your catechist about it this week.

scripture.note: God spoke in many ways, and now through his Son
Jesus explains the Scriptures on the road to Emmaus
God's tender love for Israel

sources.title: Pope Benedict XVI, Verbum Domini 42: the "dark" passages
Dei Verbum (Vatican II), 11-16

topics.q: Why not the Bible alone?
topics.short: Because the Bible never says that it alone is the rule of faith, and it could not interpret itself. Jesus founded a Church before a word of the New Testament was written, and it was the Church that recognized which books belong in the Bible. Scripture, Tradition and the Church's teaching office stand together.
steps: Jesus wrote no book. He taught apostles and sent them out to preach. For about 20 years there was no New Testament at all, yet the Church was growing.
The apostles taught both in writing and by word of mouth, and told believers to hold on to both (2 Thessalonians 2:15).

The Bible does not contain a list of its own books. That list was recognized by the Church over time and confirmed by councils around AD 400. If you trust the list, you are already trusting the Church.

When people read the Bible alone, they reach very different conclusions on baptism, the Eucharist and much more. Thousands of separate communities exist today. A living authority is needed to settle such questions.
Scripture itself calls the Church "the pillar and foundation of the truth" (1 Timothy 3:15). The Church does not stand above the Bible; it serves it, guarding and explaining it faithfully.

objections.o: Tradition is just human customs, which Jesus criticized.
objections.r: Jesus criticized human traditions that cancelled God's commandments (Mark 7:8-13). Sacred Tradition is something else: the apostles' own teaching, handed on in the Church's life, worship and faith.

objections.o: The Holy Spirit guides each believer to understand the Bible.
objections.r: The Spirit does guide each believer, but sincere Spirit-filled Christians contradict each other. Jesus promised the Spirit to lead the apostles and their successors as a body into all truth (John 16:13).

topics.think: How did the first Christians, before the New Testament was written, know what to believe?

scripture.note: Hold fast to the traditions, by word or by letter
The Church, pillar and foundation of the truth
"How can I understand unless someone guides me?"
Some things in Paul are hard to understand

sources.title: Dei Verbum (Vatican II), chapter 2: handing on revelation
Saint Irenaeus, Against Heresies, book 3, chapter 3 (about AD 180)

topics.q: Hasn't science disproved religion?
topics.short: No. Science and faith answer different questions. Science asks how nature works; faith asks why there is anything at all, and what life is for. Modern science was born largely in a Christian culture, and many of its founders were believers, including Catholic priests.
steps: Science studies the physical world by measurement and experiment. It is powerful, but its method can only reach what is physical and repeatable.
Questions such as "why is there something rather than nothing?", "what is good?" or "does my life have meaning?" are not experimental questions. Science cannot answer them, and it does not claim to.
Science itself rests on beliefs it cannot prove: that nature is orderly, that our minds can understand it and that truth is worth seeking. These fit naturally with belief in a rational Creator.

History shows partnership more than war. The Church founded the first universities. Catholic scientists include Copernicus (a cleric), Gregor Mendel (an Augustinian friar who founded genetics) and Georges Lemaître (a priest, father of the Big Bang theory).
The Church today runs the Vatican Observatory and the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, whose members include Nobel Prize winners of all faiths and none.

objections.o: What about Galileo?
objections.r: The Galileo affair was a real mistake by Church authorities, mixed with politics and personalities, and Saint John Paul II publicly acknowledged it in 1992. But it is a single painful episode, not a pattern; the Church supported astronomy before and after.

objections.o: Science explains more and more, so God is less and less needed.
objections.r: God is not a gap-filler for what science has not explained yet. He is the reason there is a world for science to explain. Knowing how an engine works does not make the engineer unnecessary.

topics.think: Which questions in your life could science answer, and which could it not?

scripture.note: You have arranged all things by measure and number and weight
How manifold are your works, in wisdom you made them all (Psalm 104 in most Bibles)
It is the glory of kings to search things out

sources.title: Saint John Paul II, Fides et Ratio (Faith and Reason)
The Vatican Observatory
Galileo affair (Wikipedia)

topics.q: Can a Catholic accept evolution?
topics.short: Yes. The Church has no problem with the scientific theory of evolution as an explanation of how living things developed. What it rejects is the philosophical claim that everything is only blind chance with no purpose. God can work through natural processes, and each human soul is created directly by God.
steps: Genesis teaches religious truths: that God created everything, that creation is good, that humans are made in God's image and that sin entered through human choice. It is not a science textbook and does not try to be.
Catholics have never been required to read the six days as six literal 24-hour days. Saint Augustine, 1,600 years ago, already read them as a way of describing God's order.
Pope Pius XII (1950) said Catholics may study evolution as a scientific question. Saint John Paul II (1996) said it is "more than a hypothesis".
A process that unfolds over time does not exclude a Creator; it may be one of the ways he works. A gardener is no less a gardener because plants grow by themselves.

What the Church insists on: God is the Creator of all, the human soul is not a product of matter but is created directly by God, and humanity truly fell from friendship with God through an original sin.

objections.o: Evolution shows we are just animals.
objections.r: We share a body with the animal world, but we can reason, love freely, create art, ask about God and know right from wrong. These point to a spiritual soul that matter alone does not explain.

objections.o: Then Adam and Eve are just a myth.
objections.r: The Church teaches that Genesis uses symbolic language, but describes a real event at the beginning of human history: our first parents' free choice against God, whose effects we all inherit.

topics.think: Does the age of the universe make God seem smaller to you, or greater?

scripture.note: Humans made in God's image
Formed from dust, given the breath of life

sources.title: Pope Pius XII, Humani Generis (1950), 36
Gregor Mendel, friar and father of genetics (Wikipedia)
Catholic Church and evolution (Wikipedia)

topics.q: Are miracles possible?
topics.short: If God exists, yes. The laws of nature describe what happens when nothing outside nature acts. A miracle is not breaking those laws so much as the Author of nature acting directly. The real question is evidence, and the Church is very careful: it investigates claimed miracles with doctors and scientists, and rejects most of them.
steps: Laws of nature tell us what normally happens. They do not forbid someone from outside the system acting. If you catch a falling apple, you have not broken the law of gravity.
If God made nature, he is not trapped by it. So miracles are possible if God exists. Whether one happened is a question of evidence.
Miracles are rare by definition. They are signs, not shows, meant to point to God and confirm his message.

The Church is cautious. At Lourdes, a medical bureau of doctors has studied thousands of claimed healings since 1883. Only about 70 have been recognized as scientifically unexplained and also religiously significant.
For a saint to be canonized, normally a miracle must be investigated by medical experts, many of whom are not Catholic, who must find no natural explanation.

objections.o: David Hume argued that a miracle is always less likely than a mistake or a lie.
objections.r: That would rule out any unusual event, however good the evidence. It assumes in advance that miracles do not happen. A fair mind weighs the evidence in each case.

objections.o: Unexplained just means we don't know yet.
objections.r: Sometimes. That is why the Church waits years and asks for healings that are instant, complete and lasting, often of conditions with well-understood courses. The point is not ignorance, but what best explains the facts.

topics.think: What evidence would you need to believe a miracle had happened? Is that a fair standard?

scripture.note: These signs are written so that you may believe
So that you may know: the healing of the paralytic
Peter heals in the name of Jesus

sources.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: miracles
Lourdes Medical Bureau (Wikipedia)

topics.q: Why do I need the Church? Isn't Jesus enough?
topics.short: Jesus is enough, and the Church is how he chose to stay with us. He did not just teach ideas; he gathered a community, gave it leaders, sacraments and a mission, and promised to remain with it until the end of time. Loving Jesus means loving what he founded.
steps: Jesus did not write a book or start a philosophy school. He chose twelve apostles, trained them and sent them with his authority: "Whoever listens to you listens to me" (Luke 10:16).
He said "I will build my Church" (Matthew 16:18), one Church, not many, and he prayed that his followers would be one (John 17:21).
He gave the Church the means to share his life: baptism, the Eucharist, forgiveness of sins. These are given in and through a community.
The New Testament calls the Church the Body of Christ. Saying "I love Jesus but not his Church" is a bit like saying "I love you, but not your body".
Faith is not meant to be lonely. We need others to teach us, correct us, pray with us and need us. No one walks to Emmaus alone.

objections.o: I can pray to God alone, at home.
objections.r: You can and should pray alone. But Jesus also commanded "Do this in memory of me" at a shared meal, and promised to be present "where two or three are gathered". Personal prayer and the Church belong together.

objections.o: Organized religion is just about power and money.
objections.r: Any human institution can be abused, and the Church's members have failed. But the Church also runs more schools, hospitals and charities than any other organization in the world, mostly through ordinary people serving freely.

topics.think: Who has helped you take a step toward God? Did you get there alone?

scripture.note: "On this rock I will build my Church"
Go and make disciples; I am with you always
One body, many parts
The first Christians, together

sources.title: Lumen Gentium (Vatican II on the Church)
Catechism 748-780: the Church in God's plan

topics.q: Why the Catholic Church and the Pope?
topics.short: Because the Catholic Church can trace itself back, without a break, to the apostles and to Peter, whom Jesus made the rock of his Church. Its bishops are the apostles' successors, and the Pope is the successor of Peter. The early Christians described a Church that is recognizably Catholic: united around bishops, celebrating the Eucharist, and in communion with Rome.
steps: Jesus changed Simon's name to Peter, meaning rock, and said "on this rock I will build my Church". He gave him the keys of the kingdom, a sign of authority from the Old Testament (Isaiah 22:22).
Jesus also asked Peter alone to "feed my sheep" (John 21:15-17) and prayed for him to strengthen his brothers (Luke 22:32).
Peter led the apostles in Acts and died as a martyr in Rome. The bishops of Rome after him were recognized as his successors.

The earliest Christian writers confirm this. Saint Ignatius (about AD 107) first used the word "Catholic" for the Church united around its bishop. Saint Irenaeus (about AD 180) listed the bishops of Rome from Peter onward and said every church should agree with Rome.

Jesus promised that the gates of hell would not prevail against his Church. A Church that has lasted 2,000 years, through persecution, scandal and the fall of empires, with the same faith and sacraments, is a sign of that promise.
Other Christians share much of this treasure, and the Church honours them as brothers and sisters. But the fullness of what Christ gave subsists in the Catholic Church.

objections.o: The rock is Peter's faith, not Peter himself.
objections.r: In Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke, the same word, Kepha, means both Peter and rock: "You are Kepha, and on this Kepha I will build my Church". The keys were given to Peter personally.

objections.o: Some popes were very bad men.
objections.r: Yes. The Pope is not promised personal holiness, only that, when he solemnly defines a teaching on faith and morals for the whole Church, God will keep him from error. That the faith survived bad popes intact is itself remarkable.

objections.o: Infallibility means the Pope can never be wrong.
objections.r: No. It applies only in rare, solemn definitions. The Pope can be wrong about football, politics or history, and he goes to confession like everyone else.

topics.think: What would it take for a community founded 2,000 years ago to still exist with the same faith today?

scripture.note: Peter, the rock, and the keys
Strengthen your brothers
Feed my sheep
The key of the house of David

sources.title: Saint Ignatius of Antioch, Letter to the Smyrnaeans, 8
Saint Irenaeus, Against Heresies, book 3, chapter 3
Lumen Gentium, chapter 3

topics.q: How can the Church be true when its members did terrible things?
topics.short: The sins of Church members are real and grave, and they must be named, not hidden. In Canada that includes abuse and the harm done in residential schools. But the truth of what Jesus taught does not depend on the holiness of those who fail to live it. The Church is holy because of Christ, and sinful because of us.
steps: Be honest first. Clergy abuse, the cover-ups and the Church's part in Canada's residential schools caused deep and lasting harm. Pope Francis came to Canada in 2022 and asked forgiveness from Indigenous peoples.
Jesus expected this. One of the Twelve betrayed him, and Peter denied him. He compared his kingdom to a field with weeds growing among the wheat.
Whether a teaching is true does not depend on who teaches it. A doctor who smokes does not make smoking healthy. Christ's words judge the sins of his own followers most of all.
The Church is not a club of the perfect. It is a hospital for sinners. Its holiness comes from Christ, his sacraments and his Spirit, not from the record of its members.
Look at the whole picture: alongside the scandals are countless saints, and millions of quiet Catholics feeding the hungry, nursing the sick and teaching children.
Leaving because of the sins of others gives them the last word. Many saints, like Saint Catherine of Siena, stayed and fought for reform from inside.

objections.o: If God guided the Church, these things would never happen.
objections.r: God guides the Church's teaching on faith and morals, but he does not take away the freedom of its members. He never promised a Church without sinners, only one that would not lose the truth.

objections.o: Church leaders protected abusers, so I can't trust them.
objections.r: That anger is just, and many Catholics share it. Since then, the Church in Canada has put safeguarding standards in place. Your faith rests on Christ, not on any bishop, and you can still demand that leaders be accountable.

topics.think: Can you hold together, in your heart, both grief at the Church's sins and trust in Christ who is present in it?

scripture.note: Weeds among the wheat
Jesus' warning about harming little ones
"Lord, to whom shall we go?"

Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops

topics.q: Is Jesus really present in the Eucharist?
topics.short: Catholics believe the bread and wine truly become the Body and Blood of Christ, though they still look like bread and wine. This is not a later invention: Jesus taught it plainly, the first Christians believed it, and the Church has believed it ever since.
steps: At the Last Supper, Jesus took bread and said "This is my body". He did not say "this is a symbol of my body".

In John 6, Jesus says "my flesh is true food and my blood is true drink". Many disciples were shocked and left. Jesus did not call them back to explain it was only a symbol; he let them go and asked the Twelve if they would leave too.
Saint Paul warns that anyone who eats the bread unworthily is "answerable for the body and blood of the Lord" (1 Corinthians 11:27). That makes sense only if it really is his body.

The early Christians took it literally. Saint Ignatius (about AD 107) called the Eucharist "the flesh of our Saviour". Saint Justin Martyr (about AD 155) wrote that it is not common bread, but the flesh and blood of Jesus.

How? The Church calls it transubstantiation: what the bread and wine are, their substance, becomes Christ, while what they look and taste like stays the same. It is a miracle of faith, not something we can see.
Why? Because love wants to be close. Jesus gives himself as food so that he can live in us.

objections.o: Jesus also said "I am the door" and "I am the vine". It's a metaphor.
objections.r: In those cases no one walked away shocked, and Jesus did not repeat himself more strongly. In John 6 he repeated it four times, each more concrete, and let people leave rather than soften it.

objections.o: It still looks and tastes like bread.
objections.r: Yes, and Catholics have always taught that. The change is in what it is, not in how it appears. That is why faith is needed to receive it.

topics.think: If Jesus is really there, how would you want to prepare to meet him at Mass?

scripture.note: The bread of life, and many walk away
"This is my body"
Answerable for the body and blood of the Lord
Known in the breaking of the bread

sources.title: Saint Justin Martyr, First Apology, 66 (about AD 155)
Saint John Paul II, Ecclesia de Eucharistia

topics.q: Why confess to a priest and not just to God?
topics.short: Because Jesus chose to forgive sins through his apostles. After the Resurrection he gave them the power to forgive or retain sins, which they could only do if people told them. In confession, it is Christ who forgives, and you hear the words of forgiveness out loud, with certainty.
steps: Only God can forgive sins. Jesus showed he had this power, and he chose to share it: "Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them" (John 20:23).
To forgive or retain, the apostles had to know what the sins were. That implies people would tell them.
The early Church practised confession of sins in the community and to its leaders (James 5:16), and the practice developed into the private confession we have today.
Sin is not only private. It wounds the Body of Christ. The priest represents both Christ and the Church, so reconciliation with God and with the community happen together.
There is wisdom in it too. Saying a sin out loud breaks its hold, a priest can give advice, and hearing "I absolve you" gives peace that a silent prayer often cannot.
The priest can never reveal what he hears, under any circumstances. This is called the seal of confession.

objections.o: I can confess directly to God.
objections.r: You can and should tell God you are sorry every day. Confession does not replace that; it is the gift Jesus added for when we need sure forgiveness, especially of serious sins.

objections.o: The priest is a sinner too.
objections.r: He is, and he goes to confession himself. The forgiveness does not come from his holiness but from Christ acting through him.

topics.think: What would it feel like to hear, out loud, that you are forgiven?

scripture.note: "Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them"
Confess your sins to one another
The ministry of reconciliation
The father runs to meet his son

sources.title: Catechism 1422-1498: the sacrament of Penance
Saint John Paul II, Reconciliatio et Paenitentia

topics.q: Why do Catholics honour Mary so much?
topics.short: Because God honoured her first. Catholics do not worship Mary; worship belongs to God alone. We honour her as the mother of Jesus, the first and best disciple, and our spiritual mother. Everything the Church says about Mary points to her Son.
steps: God chose Mary to be the mother of his Son. The angel greeted her as "full of grace", and her cousin Elizabeth called her "the mother of my Lord".
Mary herself foretold "all generations will call me blessed" (Luke 1:48). Catholics are simply doing what Scripture says.
Since Jesus is God, Mary is rightly called the Mother of God. This title was confirmed at the Council of Ephesus in 431, mainly to protect the truth about Jesus.
Honouring is not worshipping. We honour parents, heroes and saints; we worship only God. Catholics are taught clearly that Mary is a creature, saved by her Son.
From the cross, Jesus gave Mary to the beloved disciple as his mother (John 19:26-27). Christians have seen in this a gift to all of us.
Her role is always the same: "Do whatever he tells you" (John 2:5). She leads people to Jesus.

objections.o: Catholics give Mary the attention that belongs to Jesus.
objections.r: Love for a mother does not take away from love for her son. The Rosary, the most Marian prayer, is a meditation on the life of Jesus from start to finish.

objections.o: Mary had other children, the "brothers of Jesus".
objections.r: In Hebrew and Aramaic, the word for brother also meant cousin or close relative. The same "brothers" James and Joses are later named as sons of another Mary (Matthew 27:56). And Jesus entrusted his mother to John, which would be strange if she had other sons.

topics.q: Why pray to saints instead of going straight to God?
topics.short: Catholics do go straight to God, and they also ask the saints to pray for them, just as you might ask a friend to pray for you. The saints are alive in Christ, closer to God than ever, and still part of the one family of the Church.
steps: Christians ask each other to pray for them all the time. Saint Paul asked for prayers constantly, and James says the prayer of a righteous person has great power (James 5:16).
Death does not end the Church family. Jesus said God is "God not of the dead, but of the living" (Mark 12:27). Those who die in Christ are alive with him.
The Bible shows those in heaven praying: in Revelation, the elders offer "the prayers of the saints" before God (Revelation 5:8).
So asking a saint to pray for us is asking a friend in heaven, who is closer to God than anyone on earth, to join our prayer.
Catholics do not worship saints. Praying to a saint means asking, not adoring. Only God is worshipped.

objections.o: There is only one mediator between God and humanity, Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5).
objections.r: True, and the very next verses urge Christians to pray for one another. Our prayers for each other share in Christ's one mediation; they do not compete with it. The same goes for the saints.

objections.o: How can saints hear so many prayers at once?
objections.r: In heaven, the saints are not limited by time and space as we are. They share in God's life and see in him what he gives them to see.

topics.think: Which saint's story has touched you? Would you like to ask them to pray for you?

topics.q: What is purgatory, and why believe in it?
topics.short: Purgatory is not a second chance or a place of punishment like hell. It is God's mercy finishing his work in those who die in his friendship but are not yet fully ready for heaven. It is the final healing of love, and we can help those there by our prayers.
steps: Heaven is perfect union with God, and nothing impure can enter it (Revelation 21:27).
Many people die loving God but still carrying selfishness, bad habits and the effects of sins already forgiven. They are saved, but not yet fully healed.
It makes sense that God would finish that healing. Saint Paul describes a person who is saved "but only as through fire" (1 Corinthians 3:15).

Jews before Christ prayed for the dead (2 Maccabees 12:44-46), and Christians have done so from the beginning; inscriptions in the Roman catacombs ask prayers for the departed. Praying for the dead only makes sense if they can still be helped.
Purgatory is good news: God loves us too much to leave his work in us unfinished. Everyone in purgatory is on the way to heaven.

objections.o: The word "purgatory" is not in the Bible.
objections.r: Neither is the word "Trinity". The reality is present: purification after death, prayer for the dead, and the call to be perfected before seeing God.

objections.o: Doesn't Christ's death pay for everything?
objections.r: Yes. Purgatory adds nothing to Christ's work; it is that very work being completed in us. It is not paying a debt but being made ready for love.

topics.q: Aren't all religions basically the same?
topics.short: All religions share some true and beautiful things, and the Catholic Church respects whatever is true and holy in them. But they make different claims, sometimes opposite ones, about God, Jesus and salvation, so they cannot all be equally true. Christianity's claim is unique: God himself became man in Jesus.
steps: Religions agree on much: prayer, humility, care for the poor, the golden rule. The Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions (Nostra Aetate 2).

But they also contradict each other. Jesus either died on the cross or he did not. God is either personal or not. We are reborn many times or live once. Saying all are equally true means not taking any of them seriously.
Most religions describe people seeking God. Christianity says God came seeking us: the Word became flesh. That is either the most important event in history or it is false.
Christians believe Jesus is the way, the truth and the life, and that all salvation comes through him. That is why the Church shares the Gospel with everyone, with respect and never by force.
The Church also teaches that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know Christ, but seek God sincerely and follow their conscience, can be saved by his grace, in ways known to God.

objections.o: It's arrogant to say your religion is true.
objections.r: Every serious belief, including "all religions are equal", claims to be true. The question is not whether to make a claim but whether it is true, and whether we hold it humbly and lovingly.

objections.o: Then my family and ancestors are lost.
objections.r: No. The Church does not teach that. It teaches that God wants everyone to be saved and gives grace in ways we cannot see. We can hope for them and pray for them with confidence in his mercy.

topics.q: How do Christianity and Islam relate?
topics.short: With deep respect and real differences. Christians and Muslims both worship the one God, Creator of heaven and earth, honour Abraham, revere Mary and pray, fast and give alms. The heart of the difference is Jesus: Islam honours him as a great prophet, while Christians believe he is the eternal Son of God who died and rose again.
steps: The Church "regards with esteem" Muslims, who adore the one, living and merciful God, who has spoken to humanity (Nostra Aetate 3).

Much is shared: one God, the call to submit to his will, Abraham as a father in faith, prayer, fasting, charity, the hope of resurrection and judgment, and great love for Mary, who has a whole chapter of the Qur'an named after her.
The Qur'an honours Jesus as Messiah, born of the Virgin Mary, a worker of miracles, and even calls him a Word from God. Christians see these as true and precious.

The differences are about who Jesus is. Christians believe he is God the Son, made man, and that he truly died on the cross and rose. Islam teaches he was a prophet, not divine, and is usually read as saying he was not crucified (Qur'an 4:157).

These are serious questions of history and revelation. The evidence for the crucifixion is among the strongest of ancient history (see "Did Jesus really exist?"), and Jesus' own claims (see "Was Jesus just a good teacher?") ask us to decide who he is.

Christians understand the Trinity not as three gods but as the one God whose inner life is love (see "Three persons and one God"). That is often the biggest misunderstanding, and worth patient conversation.

objections.o: Christians changed the original Gospel.
objections.r: We have thousands of New Testament manuscripts from centuries before Islam, and they show the same message about Jesus' death, Resurrection and divine identity. There is no evidence of an earlier Gospel that said otherwise.

objections.o: If we share so much, why does the difference matter?
objections.r: Because it is about God's own self-revelation. If God truly became man and died for us, that changes how we know him: not only as Lord and Judge, but as a Father who comes in person to save.

topics.think: What do you most love from what you learned about God before? How does Jesus fulfil it?

topics.q: My family has a different faith. How do I handle that?
topics.short: With love, patience and wisdom. Becoming Catholic does not mean rejecting your family or everything you received from them. Honour your parents, keep the good of your heritage, share your faith mostly by how you live, and be prudent about when and how you speak, especially where changing religion carries real risk.
steps: The commandment to honour your father and mother still applies, and becoming Catholic should make you a more loving son or daughter, not a colder one.
Much of what you received, such as prayer, reverence for God, hospitality and family loyalty, is good and can be kept and brought to Christ.
Faith is your free choice. The Church teaches that no one may be forced to believe or to stop believing (Dignitatis Humanae), and that includes you.
Choose the moment and the words with care. Explain what drew you, not what is wrong with them. Listen as much as you speak.

Your safety matters. In some families and countries, changing religion can lead to rejection or danger. The Church does not ask you to be reckless. Talk confidentially with your priest about how and when to share.
Pray for your family every day, and let your joy, kindness and peace be the strongest argument.

objections.o: If I become Catholic, I am betraying my family.
objections.r: Following your conscience toward the truth is not betrayal. You can love your family deeply and still follow Christ. Many converts find, over time, that their love for their family grows.

objections.o: Jesus said he came to bring a sword, dividing families.
objections.r: He was warning that following him may cost something, not commanding us to cause conflict. In the same Gospel he tells us to love, forgive and honour our parents.

topics.think: What is one way you could show your family more love this week, without words?

topics.q: Why does the Church have so many rules?
topics.short: The Church's moral teaching is not a list of arbitrary rules but a map for human flourishing, drawn by the One who made us. Like the instructions that come with an instrument, it shows how we work best. At its heart are only two commands: love God, and love your neighbour.
steps: Jesus summed up the whole law in two commandments: love God with all your heart, and your neighbour as yourself. Every other teaching unpacks what love looks like in practice.
Freedom is not doing whatever we want; it is being able to do what is good. A pianist who practised is freer at the piano than someone who never accepted any rules.
God's commands protect what is precious: life, marriage, truth, the poor, our own hearts. They are fences at the edge of a cliff, not walls of a prison.
Many teachings that seem hard, about sexuality, marriage or money, make more sense when you see the vision behind them: the dignity of the person and love that gives itself fully.
The Church is a mother, not a police force. She also offers mercy for every failure through confession, and walks with people step by step.

objections.o: Who is the Church to tell me how to live?
objections.r: The Church's claim is that she passes on Christ's teaching, not her own opinions. If Jesus is who he said he is, his guidance about life is worth trusting even where we do not yet understand it.

objections.o: I agree with most things, but not everything.
objections.r: That is very common on the journey. Keep asking, read why the Church teaches what she does, and talk with your catechist. Many people find that hard teachings make sense over time.

topics.think: Which teaching of the Church is hardest for you? What is the good it is trying to protect?
